en: The Philippine eagle, known locally as the monkey-eating eagle, is the national bird and features a distinctive crest of brown feathers on its head.
Emilio Aguinaldo proclaimed Philippine independence from Spanish colonial rule on June 12, 1898, at his ancestral home in Kawit, Cavite.
The Senate of the Philippines is the upper house of Congress, composed of twenty-four senators who are elected by the entire national voting population.
The Ifugao people carved the magnificent Banaue Rice Terraces into the mountains of the Cordilleras over two thousand years ago.
During the Ati-Atihan festival in Kalibo, Aklan, participants paint their bodies with black soot and dance in the streets to honor the Santo Niño.
Pagmamano is a traditional Filipino gesture of respect where a younger person takes the elder's right hand and gently presses it to their forehead.
Dr. Ramon Barba invented a simple, affordable technique using potassium nitrate to induce year-round flowering in mango trees, boosting the Philippine agricultural industry.
Before the arrival of the Spanish, early Filipinos used Baybayin, an ancient alphabetic writing system composed of seventeen basic symbols to write their languages.
The iconic Philippine jeepney was originally created by repurposing surplus United States military jeeps left in the country after World War II.
National hero Jose Rizal wrote the novels Noli Me Tangere and El Filibusterismo to expose the abuses of the Spanish friars in the Philippines.
The sampaguita, a fragrant white jasmine flower, was declared the national flower of the Philippines in 1934 because it symbolizes purity and simplicity.
Under the Philippine Constitution, every child has the right to free and compulsory elementary education, as well as free secondary education in public schools.
